title: Genitive and dative

objectives.can: Recognise genitive and dative forms and give the commonest sense of each.

explanation.summary: The genitive is the case of 'of': it joins one noun to another. The dative is the case of 'to' and 'for': it names the person who receives or benefits. Between them they carry much of the meaning that English puts into the little words 'of', 'to' and 'for'.

sections.heading: The genitive: 'of'
body: The commonest use of the genitive is to say that one noun belongs to, or is connected with, another. In *lux hominum*, 'the light of men', *hominum* is genitive plural and depends on *lux*. The same case says what a person or thing is full of: *plenum gratiæ et veritatis*, 'full of grace and truth'.

A genitive can also name the whole of which something is a part ('some of the people'): this is called the partitive genitive. All these uses can be translated 'of', but English often needs a different word, so read the sense and not only the case. The genitive normally depends on another noun and follows it, though not always immediately.

sections.heading: The dative: 'to' and 'for'
body: The dative names the person (or thing) to whom something is given, said or done, the indirect object. In *Mulieri quoque dixit*, 'to the woman also he said', *Mulieri* is dative. It can also mean 'for the benefit of' someone, and it follows many verbs of giving, telling, helping and approaching.

The dative also expresses possession, together with the verb *sum*. Latin says 'to whom the name was John' where English says 'whose name was John'. The thing possessed is the subject of *sum* (in the nominative) and the possessor is the dative. In John 1:6, *cui nomen erat Joannes*, the relative *cui* is the dative of the possessor and *nomen* the subject of *erat*.

sections.heading: The endings
body: The table sets out the commonest endings of the genitive and dative. Many of them are shared with other cases, and the analysed texts in this library leave such forms undecided. That is why the exercises here use only forms that have a single certain reading. Three facts matter most. The genitive plural is -arum (first declension), -orum (second) or -um (third); -arum and -orum are unmistakable. The genitive singular of the third declension ends in -is. The dative singular of the third declension ends in -i.

In the first declension, the genitive and dative singular are both -ae: *gratiæ* in John 1:14 may be either, and only the sense tells which (there it is a genitive after *plenum*). The analysis leaves such forms undecided and no exercise asks about them. In the second declension the dative singular -o is the same as the ablative -o, and the dative plural -is or -ibus is the same as the ablative plural: these too are undecided in the texts.

sections.heading: Ten more nouns
body: The vocabulary of this lesson adds ten nouns to those of L1.1.1. Notice that most belong to the third declension, whose nominative is not always predictable from its genitive: *pater* has the genitive *patris*, and *nomen* has *nominis*. Dictionaries give both forms for this reason.

misunderstandings: The genitive is not always 'of'. English often turns it into 'full of', 'a kind of', or a possessive 's: read each in its sentence.
The dative is not the object of every verb. Most verbs take the accusative; a few, such as verbs of giving and telling, take a dative for the person as well.
'Dative' does not always mean 'to'. In the possessive use, the dative of *sum* means 'has': it is the owner.
Do not assume -ae is a plural. It is a genitive or dative singular, or a nominative plural, of the first declension. Context decides.

deeper.heading: The dative and the ablative
body: The ablative and the dative have identical endings in the plural of all declensions and in the singular of the second declension (-o). That is why the next lesson, the ablative, reuses endings you have met here. The older grammars treat the ablative as a merger of three earlier cases, which explains its many uses.
